definition.text: Tool Interface is the boundary through which one unit of agent work reaches tools, resources and prompts published by anyone, rather than code linked directly into the agent. This repo's own target/capability table names the governing standard against a self-run adapter directly: "Tool access | Model Context Protocol | MCP endpoint | any MCP server". The current specification's own Features section keeps three distinct building blocks behind that one catalogue: "Servers offer any of the following features to clients: Resources: Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use Prompts: Templated messages and workflows for users Tools: Functions for the AI model to execute"

evidence.quote: **Tool access** | Model Context Protocol | MCP endpoint | any MCP server

Servers offer any of the following features to clients: Resources: Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use Prompts: Templated messages and workflows for users Tools: Functions for the AI model to execute

standards.role: Governs how a unit of work discovers what it may call and what is safe to call before dispatch: the catalogue a server publishes, the three distinct building blocks behind it (tools that are called, resources that are read, prompts that are templates), and its own transport track, which has moved away from a stateful stream. Authorization for a remote server is pinned to a separate standard on file here (oauth-2-1) rather than invented by MCP itself.
standards.covers: Does not govern model access itself -- the protocol is explicitly provider-agnostic rather than a way to reach a model, which is this repo's own cap-model-access's job -- and it does not decide who inside this platform is authorized to call a tool it has declared, or what happens to a call once it fails after dispatch; both stay this repo's own policy and typed-error concerns layered around the adapter. It also does not itself define the credential-exchange mechanism -- see the oauth-2-1 entry below for that.

evidence.text: MCP publishes three distinct building blocks behind one catalogue, per the current specification's own Features section: "Servers offer any of the following features to clients: Resources: Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use Prompts: Templated messages and workflows for users Tools: Functions for the AI model to execute". It is explicitly provider-agnostic: "MCP avoids this problem by being provider-agnostic. It defines a universal protocol for exposing and accessing tools, independent of which LLM you use. The same MCP server can work seamlessly with both OpenAI and Anthropic models, no code changes required." Its transport track has moved, but not on the date a since-corrected record claimed: the specification's own changelog for the current revision states the HTTP+SSE transport was "deprecated since protocol version 2025-03-26", and its own authorization page states plainly that "Authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations" rather than mandatory -- a prior record here asserted the opposite ("OAuth 2.1 with PKCE is now mandatory for all remote MCP servers, not optional"), which the specification itself does not support.

standards.role: The authorization flow this repo's own standards catalogue ties to the Model Context Protocol for tool servers, when a server chooses to support authorization at all. A record drawn from the current specification's own authorization page states, in two adjacent MUST sentences, that a remote tool server acting as an OAuth 2.1 resource server must validate tokens and their intended audience: "MCP servers, acting in their role as an OAuth 2.1 resource server, MUST validate access tokens as described in OAuth 2.1 Section 5.2. MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience, according to RFC 8707 Section 2." A second record adds that servers must publish where to authenticate: "MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) so clients can discover the correct authorization server automatically."
standards.covers: Does not cover the catalogue, a tool's input schema, or what a call returns -- that is model-context-protocol's own role above. OAuth 2.1 is a general-purpose authorization flow, not something authored for tool access specifically; it appears as a second badge on this card because MCP's own specification pins these requirements for a remote server *when that server supports authorization* -- the specification's own authorization page states "Authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations" -- not because this element defines the flow itself.

evidence.text: A record drawn from the current (2026-07-28) specification's own authorization page states the resource-server requirement in two adjacent MUST sentences, and a second record fetched from the same page confirms the identical text also stood in the prior (2025-11-25) revision: "MCP servers, acting in their role as an OAuth 2.1 resource server, MUST validate access tokens as described in OAuth 2.1 Section 5.2. MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience, according to RFC 8707 Section 2." A third record adds the discovery half, and is explicit that the requirement predates the current revision rather than being newly introduced by it: "This was introduced in the 2025-11-25 spec but 2026-07-28 tightens it considerably. MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) so clients can discover the correct authorization server automatically."

landscape.text: The real fork in this space is standard-level rather than feature-level: a vendor's own function-calling schema versus a protocol any vendor can speak against the same server. MCP's own case against a provider's tool-calling API is that it "MCP avoids this problem by being provider-agnostic. It defines a universal protocol for exposing and accessing tools, independent of which LLM you use. The same MCP server can work seamlessly with both OpenAI and Anthropic models, no code changes required." The standard itself has not stood still on transport, though a prior version of this claim misdated the change and overstated authorization as mandatory: the current specification's own changelog states the HTTP+SSE transport was "deprecated since protocol version 2025-03-26", and its own authorization page states "Authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations" -- universal in practice among public remote servers, per this card's own oauth-2-1 standard entry, but not a spec-level mandate.

usage.text: A caller declares the tool names a unit of work needs and calls one of them by name with its arguments; it does not fetch the catalogue itself, read a schema, or name a server. This repo's own target architecture states the general design rule this follows -- this is this repo's own target, not an industry standard: "It has to be simple to use." A call outside the declared surface, or arguments a tool's own published schema rejects, is refused before it leaves the platform: "Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend."

evidence.quote: It has to be simple to use.
Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend

gaps.what: A 2026-09-10 repair pass fetched the Model Context Protocol specification directly (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28, its /changelog, and its /basic/authorization page, all status=fetched, fetch_tool=markdown, in kb/research/refmodel-3-5-tool-interface.jsonl) and confirmed 2026-07-28 is the current revision (a sibling pass found /specification/latest byte-identical to /specification/2026-07-28). This closes the prior 'no fetched record exists' and 'which revision is current' gap for four of the five mechanisms this card cites against the standard (the Features building blocks, the SSE-deprecation date, OAuth being optional at the spec level, and the OAuth 2.1 resource-server Token Handling MUST sentences, the last confirmed byte-identical on both the 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 authorization pages). It does not close the gap for the MCP Registry, whose only fetched record (registry/about) carries no revision or date at all -- there is nothing to pin it to.
gaps.why_it_matters: The same repair also found that two of the records this card previously cited for the SSE-deprecation date and the OAuth-mandatory claim were flatly contradicted by their own cited page (wrong date, and 'mandatory' where the source says 'OPTIONAL'), and a third fabricated a launch date, a version-freeze string and a status-as-of date for the MCP Registry that appear nowhere on its page -- a caller who trusted the old citations without checking the source would have shipped all three errors. The fix closes those specific instances, but nothing here guarantees every remaining citation on this or other cards is verbatim; that is what tools/verify_snippets.py exists to keep checking.
gaps.research_query: the MCP Registry's own about page carries no version string or effective date to verify against; if the registry ever publishes one (e.g. leaving preview for general availability), re-fetch and re-cite against that milestone

gaps.what: This repo's own inventory of what is defined but not running records the actual MCP endpoint on this host as "MCP endpoint | Live and authenticated, zero tools registered" -- reachable and authenticated, but with nothing registered into it. The 'built' status on this card rests on the interface being proven (the harness below), not on that real endpoint having ever served a real tool.
gaps.why_it_matters: A caller reading only 'status: built' would assume this platform can actually reach some published tool today; the substrate this repo itself records says otherwise, and that gap is exactly why a 'built' card deserves suspicion rather than trust by default.
gaps.research_query: has any tool been registered into the live MCP endpoint this host runs since F-a6-03 was recorded, and by what count

gaps.what: harness/tool-access/test.sh, run directly for this profile, passes cleanly against its dry-run adapter, its in-process 'second' adapter, and a local OAuth 2.1 exchange run over real loopback sockets -- but the harness's own provenance record states its live adapter has never been pointed at the real endpoint PASS.md records on this host from this environment, and its 'second' adapter is a faithful stub of an externally-controlled catalogue unless the SECOND_SERVER_URL environment variable is pointed at a real, separately-hosted MCP server.
gaps.why_it_matters: The two things a 'built, swappable' status is meant to prove -- that the live path reaches a real server, and that the swap holds against a catalogue this platform genuinely does not control -- are each proven against a stand-in rather than the genuine article; this matches this repo's own STATUS row 37 finding that every harness's live adapter is claimed, not measured, against a real host.

gaps.what: The four operations this platform's client exposes (bind_server, list_tools, call_tool, read_resource) are marked proposed by the owning cap-tool-access skill itself rather than read off the standard's own operation names, and the specific refusal type its own worked example names for an undeclared tool (urn:agentic:problem:tool-not-declared) is pending registration in cap-errors' closed registry; the harness substitutes the already-registered policy-denied type in the meantime.

gaps.what: The reference model already carries a separate card (base.5, "Registry", status planned) for discovering models, prompts, tools and datasets. This card's own tools list includes the MCP Registry, and its own note on that entry says it is 'not itself a tool-serving endpoint' -- meaning it does not actually fill this card's slot (reaching a tool) and more properly belongs to the discovery card instead.
gaps.why_it_matters: Listing a discovery service under a card about reaching tools blurs a seam this repo says matters elsewhere: which card owns 'finding what exists' versus 'calling what you already know the name of'. Left unresolved, a reader could conclude tool discovery is this card's job when the model already assigns it elsewhere.
